---
title: "Inference"
description: "Estimate model parameters from data with established simulation-based inference methods, with joshpy running and recording every simulation"

## Why simulation-based inference

A Josh model is a stochastic simulator. Each run is one draw from a distribution
of outputs that can be sampled but not written down, so the likelihood of the
observed data can't be computed directly [@hartig2011; @cranmer2020].
Simulation-based inference estimates parameters from simulations alone: it
compares simulated output with observed data and keeps the parameter values that
reproduce it.

These pages estimate the **distribution** of parameter values consistent with
the data, not one best fit. For a single best fit, see
[Adaptive Parameter Optimization](../tutorials/adaptive-sweep.qmd).

## Who does what

- **The inference method comes from established packages.** `SbiStrategy` runs
  the [sbi](https://sbi.readthedocs.io/) package [@boelts2025], which owns the
  algorithm: proposals, weights and tolerances. joshpy implements no statistics
  of its own.
- **joshpy owns the simulations.** Each batch of parameter sets the method
  proposes is rendered, run (locally, remotely or on Kubernetes), registered,
  loaded and summarized, exactly like a sweep.
- **The registry is the only store.** Every simulation, accepted or not, is a
  registered run you can query later. Runs are content-addressed, so an
  interrupted search resumes by reusing completed runs, and a seeded search
  replays exactly.

## Notation

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| $\theta$ | Model parameters ($\varphi$ in @hartig2011) |
| $D_\text{obs}$, $D_\text{sim}$ | Observed and simulated data |
| $S_\text{obs}$, $S_\text{sim}$ | Their summary statistics |
| $d(\cdot, \cdot)$ | Distance between summaries |
| $\varepsilon$ | Tolerance |
| $p(\theta)$ | Prior |
| $p(D_\text{obs} \mid \theta)$ | Likelihood, intractable for a stochastic simulator |
| $p(\theta \mid S_\text{obs})$ | The posterior that ABC approximates |

## Three steps

@hartig2011 organize inference for stochastic simulation models in three steps:

| Step | What it does |
|------|--------------|
| **Aggregation** | Reduce simulated and observed data to summary statistics $S$, computed the same way for both |
| **Likelihood approximation** | Approximate the likelihood of $S_\text{obs}$ at a single $\theta$ from simulations |
| **Sampling** | Explore $\theta$ efficiently to recover the shape of the likelihood or posterior |

They give four options for the middle step, which differ in where the
variability comes from:

| Option | Variability comes from | Example |
|--------|------------------------|---------|
| (a) Nonparametric | Within the stochastic simulation | ABC: a simulation counts as a match if $d(S_\text{sim}, S_\text{obs}) \le \varepsilon$ [@toni2009; @beaumont2009] |
| (b) Parametric | Within the simulation, through an assumed distribution | Synthetic likelihood [@wood2010] |
| (c) External error model or informal likelihood | Outside the simulation | An explicit observation-error model; the ABC tolerance read this way [@wilkinson2013] |
| (d) Rejection filter | Either, depending on the filter criteria | Keep the parameter sets whose output meets stated criteria |

## Methods available

| Method | `SbiStrategy` | Notes |
|--------|---------------|-------|
| Rejection ABC | `method="mcabc"` | One filter over prior draws |
| Sequential Monte Carlo ABC | `method="smcabc"` | Generations that tighten the tolerance, with importance weights [@toni2009; @beaumont2009] |
| Neural likelihood, ratio and posterior estimators | Not yet | Learn a surrogate from simulations; trained on prior draws, they apply to new observations without new simulations [@cranmer2020] |

## Roadmap

The pages in this section build toward fitting a Joshua tree model to I&M
survey data, using the ForeverTree model as a known
truth:

1. **[ForeverTree case study](forevertree.qmd)**: the model, a simulated
   survey, prior simulations, and choosing summary statistics.
2. **SMC-ABC on a simulated survey**: option (a), with a sufficiency test and a
   coverage check.
3. **Rejection filter on a model property**: option (d), asking which
   parameters produce a target behaviour.
4. **Posterior probability of a model property**: combining the two.

| ForeverTree example | Joshua tree case |
|---------------------|------------------|
| Survey of fixed cells with measurement error | I&M sites, plot sizes, stage classes, detection |
| Mean height and CV of the surveyed cells | Log juvenile:adult ratio; optionally density or the spread between sites |
| Final window of the same run | End window of a separate long spin-up under normal climate |
| Annual height gain inside a band | Log λ inside $[-\delta, \delta]$ |
| Within-window SD of the gain | The "not chaotic" criterion |
| Truth outside the band | A declining truth: P(stable \| I&M) should come out low |
